content: Periodic acid is a chemical compound with the formula HIO₄ or H₅IO₆. In dilute solutions, periodic acid dissociates into hydrogen ions (H⁺) and periodate ions (IO₄⁻). When the solution becomes more concentrated, orthoperiodic acid (H₅IO₆) is formed, which can be isolated as a crystalline solid. Orthoperiodic acid can undergo dehydration to yield metaperiodic acid (HIO₄). Upon further heating, it decomposes to produce diiodine pentoxide (I₂O₅) and oxygen gas. Interestingly, the anhydride form, known as diiodine heptoxide, does not naturally occur but can be synthesized artificially. There are two distinct forms of periodates: one associated with the acid HIO₄, and the other with H₅IO₆. The former leads to the formation of metaperiodates, which contain less water (as indicated by the prefix meta-), while the latter results in orthoperiodates, which contain more water (as indicated by the prefix ortho-). Metaperiodates exhibit solubility and chemical properties similar to perchlorates, although they are less oxidizing and have a larger ionic size compared to perchlorates. Periodic acid is also widely utilized in organic chemistry, particularly for structural analysis. It has the ability to cleave vicinal diols (diols with hydroxyl groups on adjacent carbons) into two aldehyde fragments. This reaction is especially valuable in determining the structure of carbohydrates. It is worth noting that the name periodic acid is not derived from the word period but rather from iodine. The correct pronunciation is per-iodic, analogous to iodic acid or perchloric acid, and not as in the common usage of the word periodic.
